name: Foix-Chavany-Marie syndrome

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical diagnosis based on opercular syndrome features

criteria.description: Bilateral voluntary paralysis of facial, buccal, pharyngeal, and masticatory muscles with preserved automatic and reflex movements
Preservation of limb motor strength and coordination
No evidence of lower motor neuron bulbar palsy
Bilateral lesions of the anterior opercular cortex on MRI or CT
Preservation of involuntary emotional facial movements despite voluntary paralysis

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of bilateral voluntary paralysis of facial, buccal, pharyngeal, and masticatory muscles with preserved limb motor function and absence of bulbar lower motor neuron signs
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is clinical and supported by neuroimaging; differentiation from bulbar palsy is essential

laboratory: CSF analysis usually unremarkable unless underlying etiology present
imaging: Bilateral lesions in the anterior opercular cortex on MRI or CT
Possible ischemic or inflammatory changes in opercular regions
genetic: No specific genetic mutation identified; usually acquired
Rare familial cases reported but no definitive genetic marker
other: Electromyography shows preserved peripheral nerve function
Normal brainstem reflexes despite voluntary paralysis

distinguishingFeatures: Lower motor neuron signs affecting cranial nerves
Complete paralysis of voluntary muscles except vertical eye movements
Progressive upper and lower motor neuron signs
No preservation of automatic facial movements

redFlags: Sudden onset of bilateral facial paralysis
Loss of automatic emotional facial movements
references: Benson DF, et al. Foix-Chavany-Marie syndrome: clinical and anatomical study. Neurology. 1979.
Kumar N. Anterior opercular syndrome (Foix-Chavany-Marie syndrome). Neurol Clin. 2009.
Orphanet: Foix-Chavany-Marie syndrome. Orphanet Report Series. 2021.
